collection.title: Artificial Intelligence: Understanding and Using AI Wisely

questions.module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.section_skill: Describe AI as a broad term for systems that do thinking-like tasks
questions.outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
questions.intro: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks we usually connect with human thinking, such as recognizing speech, sorting photos, predicting what comes next, recommending a song, or writing a paragraph. It is an umbrella term, not one machine: a spam filter, a map app's travel-time estimate and a chatbot can all be called AI, yet they work differently and do different jobs. Calling something "AI" does not tell you how well it works or what it can do. To understand a tool, ask what task it performs, what it takes in, and what it gives back.

questions.feedback: AI is an umbrella term for many kinds of systems that do thinking-like tasks.

wrong_choices.text: Any computer program at all, including a basic pocket calculator

wrong_choices.text: A single website that answers questions in a chat window
wrong_choices.why_wrong: chatbots are only one kind of AI

wrong_choices.text: One specific robot that thinks in exactly the same way as a person
wrong_choices.why_wrong: AI is a broad group, not one robot

questions.module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.section_skill: See "AI" as a broad label, like the word "vehicle"
questions.outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
questions.intro: Think of the word VEHICLE. A bicycle, a bus and a cargo ship are all vehicles, but you would not expect a bicycle to cross an ocean. "Vehicle" names a broad group, not one machine, and knowing that something is a vehicle tells you little about its speed or range. "AI" works the same way. It names a broad group of computer systems that do tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating. Knowing that something is "AI" tells you little about what it can do. You learn more by asking what job it does.

choices.text: Both words describe ways of moving people around
Both words describe one machine with many parts
Both words name a broad group of different things
Both words describe machines that have engines

questions.correct_answer: Both words name a broad group of different things
questions.feedback: Each word covers many different things that work differently.

Both words describe one machine with many parts
wrong_choices.why_wrong: both name groups, not one machine

wrong_choices.text: Both words describe machines that have engines
wrong_choices.why_wrong: many AI systems are not machines with engines

questions.module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.section_skill: Look past an "AI" label when a decision matters
questions.outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
questions.intro: Because "AI" is a broad label, it is used loosely. Marketers may call a simple fixed rule "AI" to sound modern, and some tools that do use learned patterns never mention AI at all. Two products both described as "AI-powered" can differ greatly in quality, cost and risk. When a claim matters, for example when a school, employer or bank says AI helps make a decision, look past the label: ask what the system does, what information it uses, how it was tested, and who checks its results. A label is a starting point for questions, not an answer.
questions.prompt: A budgeting app calls itself "AI-powered," but it only applies one fixed rule: save 10 percent of each deposit. What is the best conclusion?

choices.text: It is more reliable because it says "AI-powered"
The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work
It must be learning from millions of other users' data
It cannot work, since it is not "real" AI

questions.correct_answer: The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work
questions.feedback: Labels are used loosely; look at what the system actually does.

wrong_choices.text: It is more reliable because it says "AI-powered"
It must be learning from millions of other users' data
It cannot work, since it is not "real" AI
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a fixed rule can work fine

questions.outcome_title: Explain machine learning and deep learning as nested ideas, with deep learning using many-layered neural networks
questions.intro: MACHINE LEARNING is a way of building AI in which a system improves at a task by learning patterns from data instead of following only hand-written rules. DEEP LEARNING is one kind of machine learning. It uses NEURAL NETWORKS: many connected layers of simple math units. Each layer passes numbers to the next, and early layers pick up simple features while later layers combine them into more complex ones. "Deep" means many layers, not deep understanding. So the ideas nest like boxes: deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI. Not all AI uses machine learning, and not all machine learning is deep learning.

questions.outcome_title: Explain machine learning and deep learning as nested ideas, with deep learning using many-layered neural networks
questions.intro: People often use these terms loosely, so read claims carefully. "Neural network" borrows a word from biology, but these networks are math, not brains: the comparison helped early researchers and can mislead beginners. "Deep" counts layers; it does not mean wise or thoughtful. Deep learning often needs much more data and computing power than simpler machine learning, and simpler methods can work as well on small, tidy problems such as predicting sales from a few numbers. Choosing an approach depends on the task, the data available and the need to explain results.

questions.outcome_title: Classify an AI use as recommending, recognizing, forecasting or generating
questions.intro: Most everyday AI does one of four kinds of jobs. RECOMMENDING suggests items you might want, such as videos, products or friends. RECOGNIZING (also called classifying) puts input into categories: a face in a photo, a spoken word, a fraudulent payment. FORECASTING predicts a number or event, such as tomorrow's temperature, travel time or next month's sales. GENERATING creates new content: text, images, audio or code. One app can do several jobs, for example recognizing your voice and then generating a reply. Naming the job helps you decide what could go wrong and how to check the result.

wrong_choices.text: Forecasting

wrong_choices.text: Generating
wrong_choices.why_wrong: it is not creating new content

questions.outcome_title: Classify an AI use as recommending, recognizing, forecasting or generating
questions.intro: Think of four helpers in a shop. The SALES CLERK says, "People who bought this also liked that": recommending. questions.section_skill: Decide whether a task needs prediction or generation
questions.outcome_title: Decide whether a task needs new content generated or a label or number predicted, and name a typical failure of each
questions.intro: Two broad uses of AI are easy to confuse. PREDICTIVE (or classifying) uses produce a LABEL or a NUMBER about the input: "spam or not spam," "92 percent likely to be a cat," "about 30 minutes." GENERATIVE uses produce NEW CONTENT: a paragraph, a picture, a song, a block of code. They fail differently. A prediction can be the wrong label or a number that is off. Generated content can look polished while containing false facts, invented details or material too close to someone else's work. Before using AI, ask: do I need a label or a number, or do I need new content?

wrong_choices.text: Generative: it creates new categories each day

questions.intro: A MODEL is the trained part of an AI system: the learned patterns that turn input into output. A PRODUCT (an app, website or feature) wraps a model with other parts: a screen to type in, instructions the company adds, safety filters, tools such as web search, saved settings, and usage limits. The same model can sit inside several products that behave differently, and one product can switch models over time. So "this chatbot did X" does not mean every chatbot does X, and a product's feature, like saving files or browsing the web, may come from the product, not from the model itself.

questions.section_skill: Apply the model and product distinction
questions.outcome_title: Tell an AI model from the app or service built around it, and avoid assuming that all AI systems or all chatbots behave the same way
questions.intro: A MODEL is the trained part of an AI system: the learned patterns that turn input into output. A PRODUCT (an app, website or feature) wraps a model with other parts: a screen to type in, instructions the company adds, safety filters, tools such as web search, saved settings, and usage limits. The same model can sit inside several products that behave differently, and one product can switch models over time. So "this chatbot did X" does not mean every chatbot does X, and a product's feature, like saving files or browsing the web, may come from the product, not from the model itself.

A chatbot is a model with no product around it

questions.feedback: Products and models vary, so behavior varies.

A chatbot is a model with no product around it

questions.intro: People often compare AI with humans: "it reads," "it thinks," "it is like a student." Comparisons can help explain a new idea, but they can also mislead. A system may beat experts at one narrow task, such as spotting a pattern in thousands of images, yet fail at something a child finds easy, like counting objects in an unusual picture. Treat a human comparison as a starting point, then check how the system actually performs on the task you care about.

questions.intro: Human comparisons shape trust. If a system "sounds like a person," people may assume it has human judgment, feelings or common sense. Some language models are trained to sound helpful and friendly, which can make errors easier to miss. On the other hand, dismissing a system as "just a machine" can hide real abilities and real risks. A better habit is to describe what was observed: "It summarized these ten reports accurately but invented one date," rather than "It is smart" or "It is dumb." Specific observations can be checked.

questions.intro: Human comparisons shape trust. If a system "sounds like a person," people may assume it has human judgment, feelings or common sense. Some language models are trained to sound helpful and friendly, which can make errors easier to miss. On the other hand, dismissing a system as "just a machine" can hide real abilities and real risks. A better habit is to describe what was observed: "It summarized these ten reports accurately but invented one date," rather than "It is smart" or "It is dumb." Specific observations can be checked.

questions.section_skill: Describe parameters as learned settings that capture patterns
questions.outcome_title: Describe parameters as the adjustable numbers a model sets during training, and explain that the model keeps learned patterns, not a copy of every example
questions.intro: During training, a model adjusts a huge set of numbers called PARAMETERS (sometimes called weights). You can picture them as millions or billions of tiny dials. Each time the model's output is wrong on a training example, the dials are nudged a little so that next time the output is closer. After enough nudges, the dial settings capture PATTERNS in the data, for example which pixel shapes usually mean "cat." The model keeps the dial settings, not a neat copy of every example, although it can sometimes reproduce pieces of text or images it saw many times. More parameters can capture more patterns, but size alone does not guarantee better results.

questions.section_skill: Explain training, validation and test data
questions.outcome_title: Explain why data is split into training, validation and test sets and why test data must stay unseen during training
questions.intro: Builders usually split their data into three parts. The TRAINING SET is what the model learns from. The VALIDATION SET is used during development to compare versions and settings, like practice quizzes. The TEST SET is kept aside and used only at the end to measure how well the finished model does on examples it has never seen. If test examples leak into training, the test score looks better than the model really is, because the model may have learned those exact answers. A trustworthy result comes from examples that stayed unseen.

questions.outcome_title: Recognize overfitting (doing well on familiar examples but poorly on new ones) and what good generalization looks like
questions.intro: A model GENERALIZES when it does well on new examples, not just the ones it trained on. OVERFITTING is the opposite: the model fits its training examples so closely, including their accidents and noise, that it does worse on new ones. A sign of overfitting is a big gap: very high accuracy on training data but much lower accuracy on validation or test data. questions.section_skill: Diagnose overfitting from results
questions.outcome_title: Recognize overfitting (doing well on familiar examples but poorly on new ones) and what good generalization looks like
questions.intro: A model GENERALIZES when it does well on new examples, not just the ones it trained on. OVERFITTING is the opposite: the model fits its training examples so closely, including their accidents and noise, that it does worse on new ones. A sign of overfitting is a big gap: very high accuracy on training data but much lower accuracy on validation or test data. For example, a model that learned "all photos of wolves have snow" might label a husky in snow as a wolf. Remedies include more varied data, simpler models and stopping training before it memorizes.

questions.section_skill: Tell overfitting from underfitting and a changed world

questions.intro: Overfitting is not the only way a model can disappoint. A model can also UNDERFIT: it is too simple or trained too little, so it does poorly even on its training data. questions.set_title: Fine-tuning versus giving information in a request
questions.section_skill: Tell fine-tuning from supplying information in a request
questions.outcome_title: Tell fine-tuning (further training that changes a model) from supplying information in a request (which does not change the model)

questions.intro: Choosing between the two depends on the job. For facts that change often, like this week's prices or a policy updated monthly, supplying current information in the request is usually easier to keep up to date. Fine-tuning suits teaching a lasting style or format across many uses, or a specialized task with lots of examples. Fine-tuning is NOT a reliable way to make a model "know" a long list of changing facts, and it can introduce new mistakes. Either way, results need testing, and private data used for fine-tuning needs the same care as any other data sharing.

questions.set_title: What a large language model is
questions.section_skill: Describe what a large language model does
questions.outcome_title: Describe a large language model (LLM) as a model trained on large amounts of text to predict likely next pieces of text, and say what that does and does not imply
questions.intro: A LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL (LLM) is a model trained on enormous amounts of text to do one core job: given some text, predict a likely next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, produces sentences, answers, stories or code. Because it learned from so much writing, an LLM can imitate many styles and often produces useful, relevant text. But predicting likely text is not the same as looking up facts or reasoning like a person. An LLM has no built-in way to check truth, so its output can be plausible and wrong. "Large" refers to the size of the model and its training data.
questions.prompt: What is the core job a large language model is trained to do?

choices.text: Store a copy of the internet to read from
Predict a likely next piece of text
Look up each answer in a database of verified facts
Follow a fixed rule list written by programmers

wrong_choices.why_wrong: it is a trained model, not a stored copy

wrong_choices.text: Look up each answer in a database of verified facts
wrong_choices.why_wrong: it predicts text; it does not check facts

wrong_choices.text: Follow a fixed rule list written by programmers

Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, produces sentences, answers, stories or code. Because it learned from so much writing, an LLM can imitate many styles and often produces useful, relevant text. But predicting likely text is not the same as looking up facts or reasoning like a person. An LLM has no built-in way to check truth, so its output can be plausible and wrong. "Large" refers to the size of the model and its training data.

questions.intro: People sometimes describe LLMs with extreme claims: "it is just autocomplete, so it can do nothing useful," or "it knows everything, so it is always right." Both mislead. questions.section_skill: Explain tokens and why counts differ from words
questions.outcome_title: Explain tokens as the pieces of text a language model reads and writes, and why token counts differ from word counts
questions.intro: Language models do not read words the way people do. They read and write TOKENS: chunks of text that may be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. A common word like "the" is often one token, while a long or rare word like "unbelievably" may be split into several. For English, one provider's rule of thumb is about 4 characters, or about three quarters of a word, per token, but the exact count depends on the model. Token counts matter because limits on how much text a model can handle, and many usage prices, are measured in tokens, not words.

questions.intro: A simple estimate turns words into tokens. One provider's rule of thumb for English is that a token is about three quarters of a word. To estimate tokens from words, DIVIDE the number of words by 0.75, which is the same as multiplying by 4 and then dividing by 3. Example: 60 words / 0.75 = 80 tokens. To estimate words from tokens, MULTIPLY tokens by 0.75. Example: 200 tokens x 0.75 = 150 words. These are rough estimates for ordinary English, not exact counts.

questions.intro: At each step, a language model gives every possible next token a PROBABILITY: how likely it is to come next. questions.intro: Variation has practical effects. If you ask the same factual question twice and get two different numbers, at most one can be right, and maybe neither, so the difference is a signal to check a source, not to pick the one you like. questions.outcome_title: Explain a context window as the limited amount of text a model can consider at once and predict what happens when a conversation or document exceeds it
questions.intro: A model can only consider a limited amount of text at once, called its CONTEXT WINDOW, measured in tokens. The context usually includes instructions the product adds, the conversation so far, any files or pasted text, and the reply being written. When a long conversation or document exceeds the window, something has to give: depending on the product, older messages may be dropped or shortened, part of a file may be left out, or the request may be refused. The model cannot use text that is no longer in its context, so it may "forget" early details or miss the end of a long document.

questions.set_title: What a model learned versus what you supply
questions.section_skill: Tell built-in knowledge from supplied or retrieved information
questions.outcome_title: Tell knowledge learned in training (with a cutoff date) from information supplied or retrieved during a request
questions.intro: A model's built-in knowledge comes from its training data, which stops at a TRAINING CUTOFF date. It does not know about events after that date unless the information is SUPPLIED or RETRIEVED during your request: you paste a document, or the product runs a web search and adds the results to the context. These are different: built-in knowledge is patterns frozen at training time and may be incomplete or wrong, while supplied or retrieved text is current material the model reads now, which is only as good as its source. When an answer depends on recent facts, know which kind you are getting.

questions.section_skill: Tell conversation context from saved memory
questions.outcome_title: Tell the text in the current conversation from product features that save information between conversations, and check a product's own settings
questions.intro: Two different things can make a chatbot seem to "remember." CONVERSATION CONTEXT is the text of the current chat that is sent back to the model with each message, so it can refer to what you said earlier in that chat. SAVED MEMORY (or history features) is something a PRODUCT may offer: it stores notes or past chats and adds them to future conversations. Saved memory is a product feature, it varies between products, and it can usually be viewed, turned off or deleted in settings. Neither one retrains the model. Check what a specific product saves rather than assuming.

questions.set_title: A product is more than its model

questions.outcome_title: Explain that a product adds its own instructions, settings, tools and limits, so a general description of LLMs cannot predict one product's behavior
questions.intro: A general description of language models cannot tell you exactly how a particular product will behave. Products add their own layers: SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS the company writes (for example, "be brief" or "do not give medical diagnoses"), SAFETY FILTERS, TOOLS such as web search, code running or file reading, SETTINGS, and LIMITS on length or usage. Two products built on similar models can therefore refuse different requests, format answers differently, or have different abilities. To know what a product does, test it on your task and read its documentation.
